notes.meaning: The neighbors of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned Jewish exiles had begun rebuilding a temple for the Lord. These neighbors were mainly Samaritans, a mixed people who had been moved into the land by Assyrian rulers centuries earlier. They were called enemies because they opposed the true worship of God.

These neighbors approached Zerubbabel and the family leaders, asking to join in the building project. They claimed they prayed to the same God and had offered sacrifices to Him for a long time. However, their worship was mixed with idols, and their true goal was to slow down and disrupt the work from the inside.

Zerubbabel, the high priest Jeshua, and the family leaders firmly refused to let them join. They explained that only the Jewish people were given the command by King Cyrus of Persia to rebuild God's house. Joining with idol worshipers would have corrupted God's holy temple and ruined their pure worship.

When their offer was rejected, the surrounding peoples showed their true colors. They tried to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to keep building. Their open hostility proved that their earlier offer of friendship was only a trick to ruin the work.

The enemies went even further by hiring advisers and legal agents to work against the Jews at the Persian court. They used bribery and false reports to stall the rebuilding effort. This political meddling dragged on through the rest of King Cyrus's reign all the way to the reign of King Darius.

Years later, at the start of King Xerxes's reign, the enemies wrote another official accusation against the people of Judah. This notice jumps ahead in time to show how the neighboring people never stopped trying to hurt the Jews. Even long after the temple was finished, their hatred remained alive.

Later still, during the reign of King Artaxerxes, another group of local leaders wrote a letter to the royal court against Jerusalem. The letter was composed in Aramaic, the common diplomatic language across the Persian Empire. It began an official legal attack against the rebuilding of the city.

Rehum, the local Persian governor, and Shimshai, the royal secretary, wrote this official complaint to King Artaxerxes. Because of their high government ranks, their report carried great legal weight with the crown. They used their royal authority to strike against God's people.

The letter named officials, judges, and many different ethnic groups living west of the Euphrates River. These peoples had been brought in and settled in Samaria by the great Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. Listing so many nations was a tactic to make it look like the entire region stood united against Jerusalem.
The text presents an exact copy of the formal letter sent to King Artaxerxes. The writers addressed the Persian monarch respectfully as his loyal servants in the province west of the Euphrates River.

The writers warned the king that the returned Jews were rebuilding the rebellious and wicked city of Jerusalem. They claimed the Jews were already repairing the city walls and fixing its foundations. This complaint targeted the defense walls of the city, not the temple, which had already been completed decades before.

The accusers argued that if the city and its walls were rebuilt, the Jews would stop paying their taxes, duties, and tolls. They warned the king that his royal treasury would suffer heavy losses. Appealing to the king's money was a clever way to get his immediate attention.

The officials claimed they were speaking up only because they ate the palace salt and lived on the king's payroll. They argued that it would be wrong for them to sit quietly while the king was dishonored. In reality, they hid their bitter hatred behind a mask of royal loyalty.

The accusers asked the king to look into the royal historical records of earlier empires like Babylon. Those books would show that Jerusalem had often rebelled against foreign rulers, which was why it was destroyed in the past. They cleverly used historical facts to paint the current builders as dangerous rebels.

The writers warned that if Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt, the king would lose all power over the lands west of the Euphrates River. This was a wild exaggeration meant to frighten the Persian court into taking quick action. False accusations often blow small threats far out of proportion.

King Artaxerxes sent an official reply to Rehum the governor, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates in Samaria. He addressed them with warm greetings of peace before delivering his royal decision.

The king explained that their letter had been translated into Persian and read out loud in his royal court. He took their warning seriously and treated the situation as an urgent matter of state security.

Artaxerxes reported that a search of the ancient records proved Jerusalem had indeed revolted against kings in the past. The archives also revealed that mighty rulers like David and Solomon once governed the whole region and gathered taxes from surrounding lands. This ancient strength made the Persian king fear that Jerusalem might rise up and become independent again.

Artaxerxes issued a royal decree ordering the work in Jerusalem to stop until he gave further instructions. He warned his officials not to waste any time in carrying out this order so the crown would not suffer loss. Leaving the command open to future orders left room in God's timing for Nehemiah to rebuild the walls later on.

As soon as King Artaxerxes' letter was read to Rehum and Shimshai, they hurried to Jerusalem with armed force. They used their royal authority to stop the Jewish builders by threats and violence. Their speed showed how eager they were to crush the Jews and halt the work.

This verse returns to the main story of the temple, which was halted during the reign of Cyrus. The work on God's house stayed frozen until the second year of King Darius, when God raised up prophets to stir the people to finish it. Human enemies may slow down God's work for a time, but they can never stop His plan.
